blocks.text: Chapter 5.
Scheduling: What to Do, in What Order
Fifth night, friend — and it opens a hundred million miles away, on the rust-red plains of Mars.

July 1997. NASA's Pathfinder has just pulled off a flawless landing — bouncing down in airbags, unfolding like a metal flower, sending home pictures that made the whole Earth look up. And then, days into the mission... the spacecraft starts rebooting itself. Spontaneously. Again and again, losing whole days of priceless science. Nothing is broken. Every component works. And yet somewhere inside, the machine has tied itself into a knot — a knot, friend, that has nothing to do with space and everything to do with a question you face every morning over coffee: what should I do first?
Hold Mars — we'll come back to save the mission. First, the earthbound mathematics of the to-do list.
First decide what "best" means

Here's the insight the whole field stands on: for a single machine — and you are a single machine, friend, running one task at a time — every ordering of your tasks takes the same total time. So the order only matters relative to a chosen metric... and the metrics conflict. Until you decide what you're optimizing, asking for the "best" schedule is meaningless.

Care about how badly you blow your worst deadline? The optimum is Earliest Due Date: work in deadline order, ignoring how long each task takes — eat the fridge in order of expiration. Care instead about the number of things that end up late? That's Moore's algorithm: proceed by due date, and the moment you foresee a miss, throw overboard the single biggest task scheduled so far — set it aside for last, or forever. Compost the watermelon. It minimizes the count of failures, at the price of letting a few chosen tasks fail spectacularly. And notice, friend — this is the moral core of scheduling, not a technicality: EDD versus Moore is choosing between "never let anything slip far" and "let a few things die so most things live." No algorithm can spare you that choice.

When deadlines aren't the issue but the weight of things hanging over you is, the champion is Shortest Processing Time: always do the quickest task first — each completion stops one more thing from lingering. And since tasks differ in importance, the full rule is weighted SPT: divide importance by duration and work in order of importance-per-hour. The same math grades debt advice: the beloved "snowball" (smallest balance first) is pure SPT and feels wonderful — but the optimal policy weights by interest rate, highest first, regardless of size.

Pause and guess: Weighted SPT casts procrastination in a strange new light. The chronic procrastinator, busily clearing little tasks while the big one waits — what's actually wrong with their algorithm?
Ready? Here is what happened.

Nothing — except the weights. The procrastinator is often executing Shortest Processing Time faithfully, friend — but with every task weighted equally. Treat everything as equally important, and clearing trivial quick items first is mathematically correct... for the wrong objective. The bug isn't laziness — it's optimizing task count instead of importance — and the authors note the pathology can run to a genuine mania for doing easy things. The cure isn't more effort; it's better weights: work the densest task available — the most importance per hour — and let the cheap little wins wait. When new tasks land mid-flight, the rule extends cleanly: interrupt yourself only if the newcomer beats your current task on the metric; otherwise keep going — uncertainty partly vindicates staying the course. One warning from the deep theory, friend: add dependencies between tasks and almost everything becomes provably intractable — of the thousands of catalogued scheduling variants, well under ten percent can be solved efficiently. So keep your own life in the tractable zone: fewer interdependencies, a willingness to preempt, and one clear metric at a time.
The knot on Mars
Now — back to Pathfinder, rebooting itself on another planet.

Pause and guess: Every component worked. The bug was in the PRIORITIES. A low-priority weather task, a medium-priority communications task, a high-priority system task — how did they tie the spacecraft in a knot, and what fix did JPL beam across a hundred million miles?
Ready? Here is what happened.

Priority inversion. The lowly weather task grabbed a lock on the spacecraft's shared information bus... then got preempted by the medium-priority communications task, which ran long. Meanwhile the high-priority bus-management task stood waiting for the lock — held by the frozen low-priority task. The system's highest priority was effectively waiting on its lowest, friend, until a watchdog timer concluded the machine was dying and pulled the reset cord. The fix JPL uploaded to a running spacecraft on another world: priority inheritance — when a high-priority task is blocked by a low-priority one, the low task temporarily inherits the high priority, gets rushed through, releases the resource, and the knot unties. And the human translation is one of the most counterintuitive, practical sentences in this book: if a trivial task is blocking your most important work, that trivial task IS your most important work. The unanswered email holding up the launch, the errand blocking the project — do it at the priority of what it's holding hostage, instead of letting "unimportant" chores silently strangle important ones. A ranked list is not a scheduler, friend. You need rules for how priorities interact.
Guarding the quantum

One last enemy: the switch itself. Every change of task costs — a computer swaps memory; a human reloads context, and interrupted work takes real time to resume at full depth. Switching is pure metawork — overhead that produces nothing — and at the pathological extreme lies what Peter Denning named thrashing: a system so overcommitted it spends all its time swapping and none working, while feeling maximally busy. You know this day, friend — the nonstop email-Slack-meeting-fragment day that ends with nothing done. Computer science's advice for a thrashing system is beautifully counterintuitive: do less. Drop tasks. Refuse work. Even work in arbitrary order rather than paying the metawork cost of endlessly re-prioritizing.

And borrow the operating system's two defenses. The minimum quantum: Linux enforces a floor on how briefly a task may run, so each slice is long relative to the switch cost — the human version is the protected 90-minute block, and the discipline of declining any "quick" interruption that would shatter one. And interrupt coalescing: hardware batches its interruptions rather than servicing each instantly — the human version is checking email at fixed intervals, holding office hours, letting messages pool. Donald Knuth is the patron saint: he abandoned email in 1990 and processes correspondence in concentrated batches, protecting the long unbroken stretches his work demands. Choose your checking interval by the longest response delay you can honestly afford, friend — then don't look until it elapses.
Before you go

So: the "best" order doesn't exist until you choose a metric — worst lateness (EDD), fewest failures (Moore's ruthless jettison), or least lingering weight (SPT, weighted by importance-per-hour); the procrastinator's bug is weights, not will; Mars taught us that a blocking chore inherits the priority of what it blocks; and the thrashing cure is less, not more — guard your quantum, coalesce your interrupts. This week, friend: pick one metric for your list, sort by its algorithm, and treat the first trivial thing blocking a big thing as the emergency it mathematically is.

But everything tonight assumed you know your tasks — their lengths, their deadlines. Tomorrow, the deeper problem: predicting with almost nothing to go on. A stranger mentions a movie's box office; a friend's new business — how long will it last? There's a 250-year-old formula for exactly this — reasoning from a single observation — and it turns out you carry shockingly accurate versions of it in your head already... except where the modern world has quietly corrupted them. Next time: Bayes's Rule — predicting from almost nothing.
Key takeaways
No metric, no "best": every ordering takes the same total time — choose what you're optimizing before you sort anything.
EDD minimizes the worst miss; Moore's algorithm minimizes the count of misses by sacrificing the biggest offender entirely.
Weighted SPT: work by importance-per-hour — and pay the highest-interest debt first, not the smallest balance.
Procrastination is SPT with corrupted weights: optimizing task count instead of importance — fix the weights, not the willpower.
Priority inheritance, from Mars: whatever trivial task blocks your most important work becomes your most important work.
Fight thrashing by doing less: protect a minimum work quantum and coalesce interruptions into scheduled batches, like Knuth.
